stem: Arrange the parts of the human alimentary canal in the correct order from the mouth to the anus.

options.text: Mouth -> oesophagus -> pharynx -> stomach -> large intestine -> small intestine
Mouth -> stomach -> oesophagus -> small intestine -> large intestine
Pharynx -> mouth -> oesophagus -> stomach -> small intestine -> large intestine
Mouth -> pharynx -> oesophagus -> stomach -> small intestine -> large intestine

hint: Think of the tube food travels through: the throat (pharynx) comes before the food pipe.
explanation: Step 1: The canal begins at the anterior opening, the mouth. Step 2: The mouth leads to the buccal cavity, then the pharynx. Step 3: From the pharynx the oesophagus carries food down to the stomach. Step 4: From the stomach, food passes through the small intestine, then the large intestine, and finally out through the anus.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The J-shaped stomach of humans is located in which region of the abdomen?
hint: The stomach sits just below the diaphragm, mostly on the left side.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT describes the stomach as a wide, J-shaped, sac-like structure. Step 2: It is present on the left side of the abdominal cavity, just below the diaphragm. Step 3: Therefore the stomach is situated in the upper left portion of the abdomen.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The opening of the stomach into the small intestine is guarded by the:
hint: Its name comes from the pylorus, the lower end of the stomach.
explanation: Step 1: Food leaves the stomach to enter the duodenum (first part of the small intestine). Step 2: This opening is regulated by a muscular sphincter so food passes in controlled amounts. Step 3: NCERT names this guard the pyloric sphincter.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The three regions of the small intestine, in order from the stomach, are:
hint: Remember: the C-shaped part comes first, the highly coiled part comes last.
explanation: Step 1: The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal. Step 2: It begins with the short C-shaped duodenum, continues as the long coiled middle portion, the jejunum. Step 3: It ends with the highly coiled ileum, which opens into the large intestine. So the order is duodenum -> jejunum -> ileum.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: A feeling of fullness in the stomach caused by anxiety, overeating, food poisoning or spicy food is called:
hint: The name itself says digestion has gone wrong, but mildly.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT lists disorders of the digestive system with their causes. Step 2: Indigestion is described as the feeling of fullness. Step 3: Its causes include anxiety, food poisoning, overeating and spicy food - matching the question exactly.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.4 Disorders of Digestive System)

stem: The ileum of the small intestine opens into the large intestine through the:
hint: The valve's name joins the names of the two parts it connects.
explanation: Step 1: The small intestine ends with the ileum. Step 2: The ileum opens into the large intestine (the caecum region). Step 3: NCERT names the guard at this junction the ileo-caecal valve.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The small blind sac at the beginning of the large intestine is called the:
hint: It is a pouch with only one opening - food enters but cannot go back.
explanation: Step 1: The large intestine begins where the ileum opens into it. Step 2: This beginning is a small blind sac (a pouch closed at one end). Step 3: NCERT identifies it as the caecum.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The vermiform appendix arises from the:
hint: It is a narrow, finger-like tube attached to the blind sac of the large intestine.
explanation: Step 1: The caecum is the small blind sac at the start of the large intestine. Step 2: A narrow finger-like tubular projection, the vermiform appendix, arises from the caecum. Step 3: So the appendix is attached to the caecum.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The correct sequence of the parts of the colon is:
hint: Trace it: it climbs up on the right side of the abdomen, crosses over, then descends on the left.
explanation: Step 1: The colon has four parts. Step 2: It begins as the ascending colon (going up on the right), crosses as the transverse colon, descends as the descending colon (on the left), and ends in the S-shaped sigmoid colon. Step 3: Hence: ascending -> transverse -> descending -> sigmoid.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: From the outer to the inner side, the four layers of the wall of the alimentary canal are:
hint: The outermost layer is a thin protective covering, and the innermost layer touches the food.
explanation: Step 1: The wall of the alimentary canal from oesophagus to rectum has four basic layers. Step 2: From outside to inside they are: the serosa (outermost, made of squamous epithelium and areolar tissue), the muscularis, the sub-mucosa, and the mucosa (innermost lining).
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: Diarrhoea is characterised by:

options.text: Yellowing of the skin and eyes due to bile pigments
Retention of faeces within the colon as bowel movements occur irregularly
Ejection of stomach contents through the mouth
Abnormal frequency of bowel movement and increased liquidity of the faecal discharge

hint: Think of what 'loose motions' feel like - frequent and watery.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT defines diarrhoea as a disorder of the digestive system. Step 2: It involves abnormal frequency of bowel movement. Step 3: The faecal discharge has increased liquidity, and this condition reduces the absorption of food.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.4 Disorders of Digestive System)

stem: In constipation:

options.text: The stomach ejects its contents through the mouth
Bile pigments get deposited in the skin and eyes
Bowel movements become abnormally frequent and watery
Faeces are retained within the colon as bowel movements occur irregularly

hint: It is the opposite of diarrhoea - things slow down and get stuck.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT defines constipation as a digestive disorder. Step 2: In this condition faeces are retained within the colon (rectum). Step 3: This happens because bowel movements occur irregularly.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.4 Disorders of Digestive System)

stem: The irregular folds of the mucosa in the stomach are called:
hint: They are large folds of the stomach lining, not the finger-like projections of the intestine.
explanation: Step 1: The innermost layer of the canal wall, the mucosa, forms irregular folds in the stomach. Step 2: In the small intestine these become villi-like folds. Step 3: The stomach's own irregular folds are called rugae.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The absorptive surface area of the small intestine is increased by villi, which bear on their surface the:
hint: Villi are big folds; on top of them sit even tinier folds of the cell membrane.
explanation: Step 1: The mucosa of the small intestine forms villi-like folds that project into the lumen. Step 2: The cells lining the villi produce numerous microscopic projections called microvilli. Step 3: These give a brush-bordered appearance and enormously increase the surface area for absorption.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: Each villus of the small intestine is supplied with a network of:
hint: Absorbed nutrients need two exit routes: blood and lymph.
explanation: Step 1: Villi are the absorptive units of the small intestine. Step 2: Each villus is well supplied with a network of capillaries (for blood) and a large lymph vessel called the lacteal. Step 3: Absorbed substances pass into these vessels to be carried away.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The mucus-secreting cells in the mucosa of the alimentary canal are called:
hint: They are named after the shape they take when filled with mucus.
explanation: Step 1: The mucosa forms glands throughout the alimentary canal. Step 2: Mucus is secreted by goblet cells, which help lubricate the food. Step 3: Parietal and chief cells are gastric gland cells, not mucus cells.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: Brunner's glands, which secrete mucus, are located in the sub-mucosa of the:
hint: They sit in the loose connective tissue layer of the very first part of the small intestine.
explanation: Step 1: The sub-mucosa is a layer of loose connective tissue with nerves, blood and lymph vessels. Step 2: In the duodenum, the sub-mucosa contains special glands. Step 3: These are Brunner's glands, which secrete mucus.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The crypts of Lieberkuhn are:

options.text: Intestinal glands lying between the bases of the villi

hint: They are tucked into the mucosa of the small intestine, between the villi.
explanation: Step 1: The mucosa of the intestine forms glands. Step 2: These intestinal glands, called crypts of Lieberkuhn, are located in the mucosa between the bases of the villi. Step 3: Together with Brunner's glands they secrete the intestinal juice.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The number of permanent teeth in an adult human is:
hint: Count one jaw: 8 + 8 = 16 per jaw, and there are two jaws.
explanation: Step 1: The dental formula of an adult human is 2123/2123 per jaw half pattern. Step 2: Per jaw: (2+1+2+3) x 2 sides = 16 teeth. Step 3: Two jaws x 16 = 32 permanent teeth.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The dental formula of an adult human is:
hint: In each half of each jaw: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars.
explanation: Step 1: The dental formula is written as i, c, pm, m for upper/lower jaw. Step 2: An adult has in each half-jaw: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars. Step 3: This is written 2123/2123, totalling 32 teeth.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The dental formula of the temporary (milk) teeth in humans is:
hint: Milk teeth have no premolars and only 2 molars per half-jaw - fewer than permanent teeth.
explanation: Step 1: Humans are diphyodont: milk teeth are replaced by permanent teeth. Step 2: The milk set has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 0 premolars and 2 molars in each half of each jaw. Step 3: This is written 2102/2102, totalling 20 teeth.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: Human teeth are described as thecodont because:

options.text: Each tooth is embedded in a socket of the jaw bone
They are of four different types
They appear in two sets during life

hint: The word relates to how the tooth sits in the jaw, not how many sets there are.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT uses three terms for mammalian dentition. Step 2: Thecodont refers to the arrangement where each tooth is embedded in a socket of the jaw bone. Step 3: Diphyodont refers to two sets of teeth; heterodont to different types.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The term 'diphyodont' used for human dentition means:

options.text: Teeth are embedded in sockets of the jaw bone
Two sets of teeth - temporary (milk) and permanent - form during life

hint: 'Di-' means two - two sets, not two types.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT describes mammals as diphyodont. Step 2: This means two sets of teeth are formed during life. Step 3: The first is the temporary (milk or deciduous) set, replaced by the permanent set in adults.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: Human dentition is heterodont, which means the teeth are:

options.text: Of different types - incisors, canines, premolars and molars
Embedded in sockets of the jaw bone

hint: 'Hetero-' means different - here it is about the kinds of teeth.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT calls human dentition heterodont. Step 2: This means the teeth are of different types. Step 3: The four types are incisors, canines, premolars and molars, each suited to cutting, tearing or grinding.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: Which of the following is NOT a pair of salivary glands in humans?
hint: Three pairs of salivary glands exist - the odd one out belongs to the intestine.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT lists three pairs of salivary glands in the mouth: the parotids (in the cheek), the sub-maxillary/sub-mandibular (lower jaw) and the sub-linguals (below the tongue). Step 2: Brunner's glands are mucus-secreting glands of the duodenum, not salivary glands.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.2 Digestive Glands)

stem: Saliva in the human mouth is secreted mainly by the:
hint: The largest pair of salivary glands, located in the cheek, does most of the work.
explanation: Step 1: There are three pairs of salivary glands opening into the buccal cavity. Step 2: NCERT states that saliva is mainly secreted by the parotids, which are situated in the cheek region.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.2 Digestive Glands)

stem: Salivary amylase acts on starch in the mouth and converts it into:
hint: It breaks the big starch molecule into smaller sweet units, in a near-neutral medium.
explanation: Step 1: Chemical digestion begins in the oral cavity with saliva. Step 2: Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase. Step 3: At pH 6.8 it hydrolyses about 30 percent of starch into sugars (disaccharides like maltose).
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Lysozyme present in saliva acts as:
hint: Its job is protection, not digestion - it guards the mouth against microbes.
explanation: Step 1: Saliva contains electrolytes and enzymes including salivary amylase and lysozyme. Step 2: While amylase digests starch, lysozyme has a different role. Step 3: Lysozyme acts as an antibacterial agent that prevents infections.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: The small fleshy flap hanging at the end of the soft palate is the:
hint: It is the little dangling structure you see at the back of the throat.
explanation: Step 1: The oral cavity has a hard palate and a soft palate. Step 2: At the end of the soft palate hangs a small fleshy flap. Step 3: NCERT identifies this flap as the uvula.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: The pharynx serves as a common passage for:
hint: Both the windpipe and the food pipe begin just below it.
explanation: Step 1: The buccal cavity opens into the pharynx. Step 2: From the pharynx, air passes to the trachea and food passes to the oesophagus. Step 3: Hence the pharynx is a common passage for food and air.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.1 Alimentary Canal)

stem: In the stomach, HCl provides an acidic medium with a pH of about:
hint: It is strongly acidic - far below neutral - to activate pepsin.
explanation: Step 1: Gastric glands of the stomach secrete HCl along with pepsinogen. Step 2: HCl provides the acidic medium needed for pepsin action. Step 3: NCERT gives this pH as 1.8.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: In the stomach, pepsin acts on proteins and converts them into:
hint: Protein digestion in the stomach is only partial - it stops at the peptide stage.
explanation: Step 1: Gastric juice contains pepsinogen, which HCl converts into active pepsin. Step 2: Pepsin is a proteolytic enzyme. Step 3: It digests proteins into peptides (proteoses and peptones); complete breakdown to amino acids happens later in the intestine.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Rennin is a proteolytic enzyme of gastric juice that digests:
hint: It curdles milk - useful for babies whose main food is milk.
explanation: Step 1: Gastric juice contains pepsin, rennin and HCl. Step 2: Rennin is a proteolytic enzyme found in the gastric juice of infants. Step 3: It helps in the digestion of milk proteins.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: The gastric mucosa is protected from the corrosive action of HCl by:
hint: A slippery coating plus an alkaline shield keeps the acid off the stomach wall.
explanation: Step 1: HCl in the stomach is strong enough to digest the stomach wall itself. Step 2: The mucosa secretes mucus and bicarbonates. Step 3: These protect the mucosal epithelium from excoriation by the highly concentrated HCl.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Which is the largest gland of the human body?
hint: It weighs about 1.2 to 1.5 kg in an adult - far bigger than any other gland.
explanation: Step 1: The digestive glands include salivary glands, gastric glands, liver, pancreas and intestinal glands. Step 2: NCERT identifies the liver as the largest gland of the body. Step 3: It weighs about 1.2 to 1.5 kg in an adult human.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.2 Digestive Glands)

stem: Bile juice secreted by the liver is stored and concentrated in the:
hint: The liver makes it continuously, but it is stockpiled in a small sac until needed.
explanation: Step 1: The liver secretes bile juice. Step 2: The bile is not released directly into the intestine at all times. Step 3: It is stored and concentrated in a thin muscular sac called the gall bladder.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.2 Digestive Glands)

stem: The role of bile in digestion is:

options.text: Digestion of fats with its own enzymes
Emulsification of fats and activation of lipases

hint: Bile has no enzymes - it works physically on fat droplets and switches lipases on.
explanation: Step 1: Bile juice contains bile pigments, bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids, but no enzymes. Step 2: Bile helps in the emulsification of fats - breaking large fat globules into small droplets. Step 3: It also activates lipases so they can act on the emulsified fats.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: The pancreas lies in the human body:

options.text: Between the limbs of the C-shaped duodenum
Below the stomach in the pelvic region
Inside the lobes of the liver

hint: Picture the C-shaped first part of the small intestine hugging a soft gland.
explanation: Step 1: The pancreas is a compound (both exocrine and endocrine) elongated organ. Step 2: It is situated between the limbs of the C-shaped duodenum. Step 3: Its duct joins the bile duct to open into the duodenum.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.1.2 Digestive Glands)

stem: Which of the following enzymes is NOT present in pancreatic juice?
hint: Pancreatic juice digests all three food types - but the stomach's protein enzyme is not one of them.
explanation: Step 1: Pancreatic juice contains inactive enzymes: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases, plus amylases, lipases and nucleases. Step 2: Pepsin is secreted by the gastric glands of the stomach, not the pancreas.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Trypsinogen in the duodenum is activated to trypsin by:
hint: The trigger is an enzyme secreted by the intestinal mucosa itself.
explanation: Step 1: The pancreas releases trypsinogen in an inactive form to protect its own cells. Step 2: In the duodenum, the intestinal mucosa secretes the enzyme enterokinase. Step 3: Enterokinase activates trypsinogen into active trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic enzymes.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: The intestinal juice (succus entericus) is secreted by the glands of the intestine, namely:

options.text: Brunner's glands and the crypts of Lieberkuhn

hint: Its name means 'intestinal juice' - so look for intestinal glands.
explanation: Step 1: The secretions of the intestinal glands form the intestinal juice, also called succus entericus. Step 2: These glands are the crypts of Lieberkuhn and Brunner's glands of the small intestine. Step 3: The juice contains disaccharidases, dipeptidases, lipases and nucleosidases.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Lactose is hydrolysed by the enzyme lactase into:
hint: Milk sugar splits into two different simple sugars - one of them is glucose.
explanation: Step 1: In the small intestine, disaccharides are digested by disaccharidases of the intestinal juice. Step 2: Maltase gives glucose + glucose, sucrase gives glucose + fructose. Step 3: Lactase acts on lactose (milk sugar) to give glucose and galactose.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Dipeptides are finally hydrolysed into amino acids by:
hint: The enzyme's name matches its substrate: dipeptides.
explanation: Step 1: Proteins are broken down stepwise: proteins -> proteoses/peptones -> peptides. Step 2: The intestinal juice contains dipeptidases. Step 3: Dipeptidases hydrolyse dipeptides into amino acids, completing protein digestion.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Lipases act on emulsified fats and convert them, step by step, into:
hint: Fats break down through diglycerides and monoglycerides to their building blocks.
explanation: Step 1: Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets. Step 2: Lipases (from pancreatic and intestinal juice) act on them. Step 3: Fats -> diglycerides -> monoglycerides -> fatty acids and glycerol, the final products of fat digestion.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: The semi-fluid mass of partially digested food that leaves the stomach is called:
hint: It is the soupy mixture that enters the duodenum from the stomach.
explanation: Step 1: In the stomach, food mixes with gastric juice and becomes a semi-fluid mass. Step 2: NCERT calls this partially digested, acidic food mass the chyme. Step 3: The chyme then enters the duodenum for further digestion. (Bolus is chewed food in the mouth; chyle is fat-laden lymph.)
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.2 Digestion of Food)

stem: Fats absorbed in the small intestine are transported into the lacteals of the villi as:

options.text: Free fatty acids dissolved in blood

hint: Insoluble fats get a protein coat so they can travel in the lymph.
explanation: Step 1: Fatty acids and glycerol are insoluble in water, so they cannot be absorbed into the blood directly. Step 2: They are first incorporated into micelles, enter the intestinal mucosa, and are re-formed into very small protein-coated fat globules. Step 3: These are called chylomicrons, which are transported into the lacteals in the villi.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.3 Absorption of Digested Products)

stem: Monosaccharides like glucose are absorbed from the intestine by:

options.text: Active transport against the concentration gradient

hint: Glucose is pumped in even when it is already more concentrated inside the cell.
explanation: Step 1: Absorption occurs by passive, facilitated or active transport. Step 2: NCERT states that monosaccharides like glucose are absorbed by active transport. Step 3: This transport works against the concentration gradient, using energy.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.3 Absorption of Digested Products)

stem: The water-soluble end products of digestion absorbed in the small intestine are carried to the liver by the:
hint: Absorbed nutrients go straight to the liver first for processing before reaching the rest of the body.
explanation: Step 1: The absorbed water-soluble substances are transported to the tissues via blood. Step 2: They first travel through the hepatic portal vein. Step 3: This vein carries them to the liver, where they are processed before entering general circulation.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.3 Absorption of Digested Products)

stem: The large intestine mainly absorbs:

options.text: Water, some minerals and certain drugs

hint: By the time food reaches here, digestion is done - only water and salts remain to be reclaimed.
explanation: Step 1: Maximum absorption of digested food occurs in the small intestine. Step 2: The large intestine has no significant digestive activity. Step 3: Its function is the absorption of water, some minerals and certain drugs.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.3 Absorption of Digested Products)

stem: Jaundice is characterised by:

options.text: Increased liquidity of the faecal discharge
Retention of faeces within the colon
Ejection of stomach contents through the mouth
Yellowing of the skin and eyes due to deposition of bile pigments, with the liver affected

hint: It is a liver disorder - and the yellow colour gives it away.
explanation: Step 1: NCERT lists jaundice among the disorders of the digestive system. Step 2: In jaundice the liver is affected. Step 3: Skin and eyes turn yellow due to the deposition of bile pigments.
source: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Chapter 16 - Digestion and Absorption (16.4 Disorders of Digestive System)
